Summary

This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for desktop GUI automation with multimodal LLMs. The system combines three main ideas: (1) experience-augmented hierarchical planning, where a manager decomposes tasks into subtasks using web search plus retrieved prior experience; (2) continual memory construction and update via narrative and episodic memories populated through self-supervised exploration and online interaction; and (3) an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that uses screenshots plus an augmented accessibility tree and constrains actions to language-level GUI primitives. On OSWorld, the paper reports 20.58% success with GPT-4o versus an 11.21% baseline, and also shows gains on WindowsAgentArena without adaptation. The paper includes ablations and an error analysis.

Overall assessment

The paper addresses an important and timely problem: general-purpose computer-use agents operating through real GUIs. The proposed system is sensible, fairly comprehensive, and practically motivated. The strongest aspects are the integration of planning, retrieval, memory, and interface design into a coherent framework, and the empirical gains on OSWorld. The ACI design is also a useful contribution, especially the emphasis on grounding through accessibility trees and bounded primitive actions.

That said, I have reservations about the degree of novelty of the individual components, the rigor of some experimental claims, and the clarity around what exactly drives the gains. The paper is strongest as a systems paper showing that careful integration of known ideas materially improves GUI-agent performance. It is weaker if judged as introducing fundamentally new algorithmic ideas. There are also several methodological ambiguities that should be clarified for a top-tier venue.

Strengths

1. Important problem setting
Desktop GUI automation is a high-impact benchmark for agentic systems. The paper targets realistic, open-ended tasks across applications and operating systems, which is valuable.

2. Strong empirical improvement on OSWorld
The reported jump from 11.21% to 20.58% on the full OSWorld test set is substantial in absolute terms for this difficult benchmark. The gains across categories, especially Daily and Professional, are compelling.

3. Coherent architecture
The manager/worker/self-evaluator decomposition is intuitive and well matched to long-horizon GUI tasks. The distinction between narrative memory for high-level planning and episodic memory for subtask execution is reasonable.

4. Practical ACI contribution
The dual-input design using screenshot plus accessibility tree is well motivated. Augmenting the accessibility tree with OCR-derived elements is practical, and the bounded action space likely improves both safety and observability.

5. Ablation and error analysis
The paper does attempt to isolate the effects of web knowledge, memory, ACI, and hierarchical planning, and the error taxonomy is useful.

6. Cross-OS generalization
Testing on WindowsAgentArena without adaptation is a nice demonstration that the framework is not overly benchmark-specific.

Weaknesses and concerns

1. Limited novelty of core ingredients
Most components are adaptations or integrations of existing ideas: hierarchical planning, retrieval augmentation, episodic/narrative memory, reflection, self-evaluation, accessibility-tree grounding, OCR augmentation, and constrained action spaces. The paper’s main novelty seems to be the particular combination and application to GUI agents rather than a clearly new algorithmic principle. That is acceptable for a systems paper, but the paper sometimes overstates novelty.

2. Evaluation still shows low absolute performance
Although the relative gain is large, 20.58% success remains low in absolute terms. This does not invalidate the contribution, but the paper should be more calibrated in its claims about “using computers like a human.” The title and framing are stronger than the actual capability demonstrated.

3. Heavy dependence on proprietary models and external services
The system relies on GPT-4o / Claude-3.5, text-embedding-3-small, OCR, and Perplexica/web search. This raises reproducibility and attribution questions. How much of the gain comes from better prompting and orchestration around very strong proprietary models versus the proposed framework itself? The paper would benefit from stronger controls here.

4. Potential confound from online web search
Using online web knowledge is practical, but it complicates fair benchmarking and reproducibility. Benchmark tasks may involve applications or websites for which web search directly provides procedural instructions. This is useful in practice, but it also means performance may depend on retrieval quality, search freshness, and external content availability. The paper should discuss whether web search was unrestricted during benchmark evaluation and how variance was controlled.

5. Memory construction may risk benchmark contamination
The self-supervised exploration uses “top 50 most common tasks” from applications used in OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena, and environment-aware tasks are generated from initial benchmark environments. This is potentially problematic. Even if the exact test instructions differ, constructing memory from benchmark applications and benchmark initial states may leak benchmark-specific structure into the agent. The paper should be much more explicit about train/test separation and whether any benchmark test environments were used, even indirectly, to generate exploration tasks.

6. Ablation methodology is somewhat weak
The main ablations are on a 65-example subset rather than the full benchmark. That is understandable for cost reasons, but it reduces confidence. Also, some ablations combine multiple changes or compare against baselines that differ in more than one dimension. For example, the ACI-only comparisons are not fully clean from a systems perspective. Confidence intervals or repeated runs are absent.

7. Lack of statistical rigor
No variance estimates, confidence intervals, or repeated-seed evaluations are reported. Given the stochasticity of LLM agents and web retrieval, this is a notable omission. A few percentage points may not be stable.

8. Insufficient efficiency analysis
The paper itself notes that step count and wall-clock time are unaddressed. For agent systems, especially those using hierarchical planning, retrieval, OCR, and web search, latency and token cost are central. A method that improves success by using substantially more steps or much higher cost may be less compelling in practice.

9. Self-evaluator claims are underspecified
The self-evaluator is described as assessing success/failure “without any human feedback or ground truth information,” but it is unclear how reliable this is. How does it determine whether a subtask or full task succeeded? If the worker emits DONE, is the evaluator merely summarizing, or does it independently verify? This matters because memory quality depends on evaluator accuracy.

10. Some presentation and citation issues
There are several writing and formatting problems:
- Figure numbering is inconsistent in the text (Figure 7 appears to correspond to Figure 6 in the provided content).
- Fu et al. 2024a and 2024b appear duplicated with the same title.
- “Claude-3.5-Sonnet” vs “Claude-3-Sonnet” naming is inconsistent.
- Some equations and notation are awkwardly presented.
- The paper occasionally uses strong claims without enough qualification.

Detailed comments

On the technical formulation

The manager retrieves both web knowledge and narrative memory using a “How to do X” query derived from the task and initial observation. This is plausible, but the paper does not provide enough detail on:
- retrieval corpus size and indexing for narrative/episodic memory,
- number of retrieved items,
- reranking or filtering,
- prompt templates for fusion,
- how conflicting web and memory guidance are resolved,
- whether retrieval is repeated during replanning or only once.

Similarly, the worker retrieves episodic memory keyed by task, subtask, and context, but it is unclear how robust this is to paraphrase and state mismatch. Since GUI tasks are highly state-dependent, retrieval quality is likely sensitive to context representation.

The trajectory reflector is mentioned but not really evaluated independently. It is unclear whether it materially contributes or is mostly incidental.

On memory construction

The memory bootstrapping procedure is interesting, but also one of the least convincing parts methodologically. If the exploration tasks are generated from benchmark applications and initial environments, then the resulting memory may encode benchmark-specific workflows. This may still be acceptable if clearly framed as pretraining on in-domain environments, but then the evaluation is not really zero-shot in the usual sense. The paper should explicitly state:
- whether any OSWorld/WindowsAgentArena test initial states were used to generate exploration tasks,
- whether exploration was done on the same software versions as test,
- how many exploration tasks were generated,
- how many successful trajectories entered memory,
- memory sizes at evaluation time,
- whether continual updates occur across test episodes and, if so, whether benchmark evaluation is online and order-dependent.

That last point is especially important. If the agent updates memory while traversing the benchmark test set, then later tasks may benefit from earlier test tasks. This is a legitimate continual-learning setting, but it is not directly comparable to standard independent test-time evaluation unless the baseline is given the same opportunity.

On ACI

The ACI is one of the more convincing contributions. The argument that MLLMs need a language-centric abstraction layer rather than raw mouse coordinates is strong. The OCR-to-accessibility-tree augmentation is also sensible. However, I would like more quantitative evidence on:
- how often OCR adds useful elements absent from the tree,
- how often OCR introduces false positives,
- whether the gains come mainly from element IDs versus action constraints versus OCR augmentation,
- action failure rates by primitive type.

On experiments

The OSWorld result is the headline contribution and is meaningful. Still, several experimental details are missing:
- maximum step budget per task,
- whether all methods use identical budgets,
- whether web search counts toward time/step limits,
- whether prompts were tuned on validation tasks,
- whether the baseline was reimplemented or numbers were copied from prior work,
- whether the same backbone versions were used for baseline and Agent S.

The WindowsAgentArena comparison is useful but somewhat limited because the baseline uses a different overall system and possibly different assumptions. The paper acknowledges this, but the fairness caveat should be more prominent.

On error analysis

The error taxonomy is helpful, but the analysis remains fairly high level. Since execution errors dominate, it would be useful to know whether these are mostly due to:
- failure to detect action outcomes,
- repeated loops,
- premature DONE,
- inability to recover from modal dialogs,
- text entry mistakes,
- timing/synchronization issues.

This would better support the claim that ACI and hierarchical planning address the main bottlenecks.

Questions for the authors

1. Does continual memory update occur during evaluation on the benchmark test set? If yes, are results order-dependent, and how is this made comparable to baselines?
2. Were benchmark test initial environments used to generate environment-aware exploration tasks? If yes, how do you rule out leakage?
3. How many exploration tasks were generated, and what fraction produced usable narrative/episodic memories?
4. How many retrieved memory items and web results are provided to the manager/worker at each step?
5. What is the average wall-clock time, token usage, and number of environment steps per task compared to baseline?
6. How reliable is the self-evaluator? Did you manually assess whether its summaries and success/failure judgments are correct?
7. Can the gains be reproduced without online web search, or with a frozen offline knowledge source?
8. How much of the improvement comes from ACI alone on the full benchmark, not just the 65-example subset?

Suggestions for improvement

1. Clarify evaluation protocol around memory updates
This is the most important issue. Separate:
- static-memory evaluation,
- online continual-learning evaluation,
- exploration-pretrained evaluation.
Report each clearly.

2. Strengthen contamination safeguards
If exploration uses benchmark-derived environments, provide a careful leakage analysis or redesign the setup to avoid using test initial states.

3. Add efficiency metrics
Report average steps, wall-clock time, token cost, and retrieval/search overhead. Success alone is insufficient for practical agent systems.

4. Add variance estimates
Run multiple trials on at least the ablation subset and report confidence intervals.

5. Improve ablations
Disentangle ACI components:
- screenshot only vs tree only vs dual input,
- OCR augmentation on/off,
- element-ID actions vs coordinate actions,
- single-action-per-step vs chained actions.

6. Better characterize memory
Report memory sizes, retrieval hit rates, and examples of beneficial versus harmful retrievals.

7. Tone down claims
The title and conclusion should better reflect current capability. “Uses computers like a human” is aspirational but overstated given the success rates.

8. Clean up presentation
Fix figure references, duplicated citations, model naming inconsistencies, and notation.

Recommendation

Weak Accept

Rationale

I lean positive because the paper tackles an important problem, presents a coherent and practically useful system, and demonstrates a substantial empirical improvement on a challenging benchmark. The ACI framing is also valuable. However, my enthusiasm is tempered by concerns about novelty, reproducibility, possible benchmark leakage through exploration/memory construction, and insufficiently rigorous evaluation protocol around continual learning and online web search. If accepted, I would want the camera-ready version to clarify these issues substantially.

Confidence

3/5. I am reasonably confident in the overall assessment, though some concerns hinge on experimental details that are not fully specified in the manuscript.

prompt_structured_json.summary: This paper presents Agent S, an open framework for autonomous GUI-based computer control using multimodal LLMs. The system combines three main ideas: (1) experience-augmented hierarchical planning, where a manager decomposes tasks into subtasks using both online web knowledge and retrieved prior task summaries; (2) episodic and narrative memory with continual self-updating through self-supervised exploration and inference-time experience accumulation; and (3) an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) that combines screenshots with an OCR-augmented accessibility tree and constrains actions to language-level GUI primitives. On OSWorld, Agent S improves over the GPT-4o baseline from 11.21% to 20.58% success rate, and it also improves over a comparable setup on WindowsAgentArena from 13.3% to 18.2%. Ablations suggest that web knowledge, memory, ACI, and hierarchical planning each contribute to performance gains.
strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: general-purpose autonomous GUI interaction across desktop environments.
The proposed framework is modular and conceptually well organized, with clear separation between planning, execution, memory, self-evaluation, and interface abstraction.
The ACI design is practically motivated and likely useful beyond this paper; combining screenshot reasoning with accessibility-tree grounding is a sensible contribution.
Empirical results on OSWorld show a substantial improvement over the reported baseline, including a new state-of-the-art under the stated setup.
Ablation studies are reasonably comprehensive and help isolate the contributions of web retrieval, narrative memory, episodic memory, ACI, hierarchical planning, exploration, and self-evaluation.
Cross-benchmark evaluation on WindowsAgentArena strengthens the claim that the framework generalizes across operating systems.
The paper includes qualitative examples and error analysis, which improve interpretability and provide useful insight into remaining bottlenecks.
weaknesses: Absolute performance remains low (20.58% on OSWorld), so despite relative gains the system is still far from robust autonomous computer use.

Several components are combined at once, making it difficult to determine whether the main gains come from architectural novelty or simply stronger retrieval/prompting around a powerful proprietary backbone.

The self-evaluation and memory update mechanisms are only weakly validated; there is limited evidence that the stored summaries are consistently accurate or that erroneous memories do not accumulate over time.
The paper does not sufficiently analyze computational cost, latency, token usage, or step efficiency, which are especially important for GUI agents relying on repeated MLLM calls and web search.
Comparisons may not be fully controlled across all baselines, especially given differences in action spaces, grounding interfaces, and proprietary model capabilities.

The memory construction procedure uses synthetic exploration tasks derived from benchmark-related applications/environments, raising some concern about benchmark-specific adaptation and possible indirect contamination.
Methodological details for retrieval, prompting, memory size/management, and failure recovery are not fully specified in the main text, which may hinder reproducibility despite code release.
soundness_issues: The empirical methodology is generally reasonable, but some claims are stronger than the evidence supports. In particular, framing the memory update process as a form of learning analogous to hierarchical reinforcement learning is more metaphorical than rigorous, since there is no formal optimization objective or reward-learning analysis.

The self-evaluator labels success/failure and summarizes trajectories without external supervision, but the paper does not quantify evaluator reliability. If evaluator judgments are noisy, memory quality could degrade; this risk is not systematically studied.

The use of online web search during evaluation improves realism for open-world tasks, but it also introduces variability and makes strict reproducibility harder unless search results are cached or controlled.
The ablation subset contains only 65 tasks, which is understandable for cost reasons but limits statistical confidence; no confidence intervals or significance testing are reported.

Generalization claims are promising but somewhat limited: WindowsAgentArena results are better than a comparable baseline, yet still modest overall and not compared against the strongest inaccessible system.

Potential data leakage or benchmark adaptation concerns are not fully ruled out because exploration tasks are generated from benchmark-related apps and initial environments, even if not identical to test tasks.
